title: Ten Times Faster
lede: AI will make one step ten times faster. The customer waits for the whole process. Seal a number, then count the hours that never moved.

commit.title: HOW MUCH FASTER
commit.prompt: Drafting is 30 of the 100 hours. AI makes it 10× faster. How much faster is the whole process, start to done?

captions: A 10-step process: 100 hours from request to done.
AI takes drafting: 30 of the 100 hours, made 10× faster.
How much faster is the whole process? Type a number.
IBM Credit: a financing quote took 7 days, across 5 desks.
Two managers walked one through. The work took 90 minutes.
The rest was waiting. Instant work would save 90 minutes.
IBM cut the handoffs instead: 7 days became 4 hours.
Back to our process: 100 hours, one mark per hour.
AI makes drafting 10× faster: 30 hours become 3.
70 hours untouched. The whole process now takes 73.
Even instant drafting caps it at 100 ÷ 70 = 1.43×.
Monday: of every 100 hours, how many does AI touch?

brand.takeaway: The hours you don't speed up set the limit.

sources: Amdahl, G. M. (1967). Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities. AFIPS Conference Proceedings 30 (Spring Joint Computer Conference, Atlantic City, NJ, 18–20 April 1967), 483–485. doi:10.1145/1465482.1465560

Hammer, M., & Champy, J. (1993). Reengineering the Corporation: A Manifesto for Business Revolution. New York: HarperBusiness. Chapter 3, IBM Credit Corporation: six days on average, more than seven after a control desk was added; 90 minutes of actual work; turnaround cut to four hours.
Davenport, T. H., & Nohria, N. (1994). Case management and the integration of labor. Sloan Management Review 35(2), 11–23. IBM Credit: five business functions, seven days on average.
Hammer, M. (1990). Reengineering work: don't automate, obliterate. Harvard Business Review 68(4), 104–112. An insurer's application: 22 days in process, 17 minutes of work.
Gustafson, J. L. (1988). Reevaluating Amdahl's law. Communications of the ACM 31(5), 532–533. doi:10.1145/42411.42415
Vaughan, T. S. (2020). IBM Credit revisited. Journal of Applied Business and Economics (North American Business Press). A critical reappraisal of the case.
Teaching object: the 10-step, 100-hour process on this page is constructed (intake 4, queue 12, check 6, queue 10, drafting 30, queue 14, review 6, queue 10, sign-off 3, send 5 hours).
factory/FORMAT.md and docs/DECISIONS.md Q13: the commit hold and the film-mode default guess.
honest: The 100-hour process is a constructed teaching model, not a measured process; the hours were chosen so that drafting is 30 of 100 and four of the ten steps are queues.

The IBM Credit figures (7 days, 90 minutes of work, 4 hours after the redesign) are Hammer and Champy's account, repeated by Davenport and Nohria; they are not an audited study, and Vaughan (2020) argues other factors contributed. The 90-minute sliver is drawn against 7 working days of 8 hours; on the calendar it would be thinner still.

Amdahl's law holds the untouched hours fixed. In a real process a faster step can shrink a queue (fewer handoffs) or grow one (more work arriving at review). And if the work grows to fill the faster step, the limit moves (Gustafson 1988).

tryit.title: Try it
tryit.note: Of 100 hours, how many does the AI touch, and how much faster does it make them? The rest stays.
